name: Reinforcement Learner
description: Intelligence that learns through interaction with an environment, maximizing cumulative reward over time. Maps states to actions via learned policies. Mirrors how biological organisms learn from consequences — trial, error, and reinforcement shaping adaptive behavior.

core_attributes.architecture: agent-environment loop with policy and value functions
core_attributes.pattern: reward signal, temporal difference, policy gradient

computational_substrate: simulation environments, replay buffers, policy networks

scope.definition: Sample efficiency of TD-learning vs Monte Carlo returns — number of environment interactions required to achieve 90% of optimal policy performance on standard Atari games (Pong, Breakout).

evidence.source: Sutton (1988) 'Learning to predict by the methods of temporal differences', Machine Learning 3:9-44; Mnih et al. (2015) 'Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning', Nature 518:529-533.
cross_domain_examples: DQN achieves human-level Atari performance in 50M frames — TD bootstrapping enables credit assignment over 100+ step sequences
TD-learning 3-5× more sample efficient than Monte Carlo on episodic tasks with delayed rewards
animal temporal difference learning: dopamine neuron firing patterns match TD prediction error signal (Schultz 1997)

scope.falsifiability: If Monte Carlo returns achieve equivalent sample efficiency to TD-learning on delayed-reward tasks, bootstrapping provides no advantage over full-episode credit assignment.
scope.measurement_limits: Sample efficiency advantage shrinks on tasks with dense rewards (TD and MC equivalent). Deep RL (DQN) sample efficiency appears high per environment but is orders of magnitude below biological learning.

scope.definition: Convergence stability of policy gradient methods — fraction of training runs achieving >90% of maximum return without catastrophic policy collapse, using PPO on MuJoCo locomotion benchmarks.

evidence.source: Williams (1992) 'Simple statistical gradient-following algorithms', Machine Learning 8:229-256; Schulman et al. (2017) 'Proximal policy optimization algorithms', arXiv 1707.06347.
cross_domain_examples: PPO on HalfCheetah: 0.84 of runs achieve >4000 return without collapse in 1M timesteps
REINFORCE (vanilla policy gradient): 0.52 convergence rate — PPO clip constraint reduces variance
evolutionary strategy as policy gradient alternative: 0.78 convergence on same benchmarks via gradient-free optimization

scope.falsifiability: If PPO collapse rates on MuJoCo are statistically equivalent to vanilla policy gradient, the clipping mechanism provides no stability improvement.
scope.measurement_limits: Convergence stability is strongly hyperparameter-dependent — PPO sensitivity to clip range, learning rate, and batch size requires careful tuning. Performance measured on deterministic simulation; stochastic environments show higher variance.

scope.definition: Regret minimization efficiency of epsilon-greedy vs UCB exploration — cumulative regret ratio after 10,000 multi-armed bandit trials, normalized to optimal oracle policy.

evidence.source: Auer et al. (2002) 'Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem', Machine Learning 47:235-256; Lai & Robbins (1985) asymptotically efficient adaptive allocation.
cross_domain_examples: UCB1 achieves O(log n) regret vs O(sqrt(n)) for epsilon-greedy — logarithmic vs square-root scaling
Thompson sampling: Bayesian exploration matching UCB1 regret with 0.78 empirical efficiency
biological foraging: optimal foraging theory predicts epsilon-greedy-like exploration under metabolic constraints

scope.falsifiability: If epsilon-greedy with optimal (decaying) epsilon achieves statistically equivalent cumulative regret to UCB after 10,000 trials, directed exploration provides no advantage over random exploration.
scope.measurement_limits: Regret comparisons are task-specific — UCB advantage shrinks when arm reward distributions are similar. In non-stationary environments, UCB's confidence bounds require adjustment for drifting means.
